title: Fire
summary: Gather about twice what you think you need, then build and light the fire.

sections.h: Gather first, about twice what you think

list: Tinder: dry, fine and fluffy. Birch bark, dry grass, cattail fluff, resin-soaked pine (fatwood), dryer lint, cotton balls with petroleum jelly.
Kindling: dead twigs from pencil-lead to pencil thickness.
Fuel: dead wood wrist-thick and bigger. Dry wood snaps with a crack.

blocks.cap: Most failed fires run short on kindling. Gather far more than seems necessary.

steps: Clear a 10-foot circle down to bare soil, away from overhanging branches. On snow or wet ground, build on a platform of green sticks or flat rocks.
Put the tinder bundle in the centre and lean kindling around it like a teepee, with an opening facing the wind.
Light the tinder from the upwind side, then add fuel from small to large. Blow gently at the base.
Once it’s going, a log cabin of fuel stacked around the teepee burns longer and makes good coals for cooking.

blocks.cap: Start with a teepee; build a log cabin around it once it catches.

list: Ferro rod: hold the striker still against the rod, right in the tinder, and pull the rod back. Pushing the striker scatters the tinder.

blocks.cap: Pulling the rod back keeps the sparks landing exactly where the striker sits.

list: 9-volt battery and fine steel wool: touch both terminals to the wool and it ignites.
Bow drill: it works, but it takes practice. Learn it before you need it.

blocks.p: In wet weather, use standing dead wood and the dead lower branches of conifers, and split wood to reach the dry core. Birch bark burns even when damp.

blocks.cap: A platform stops snowmelt or wet ground from drowning the fire from below.

blocks.p: Never leave a fire unattended. Before you leave, drown it, stir it, and feel that it’s cold.
